newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's future leader faces first public relations row.
newsitem.headline: HK's future leader faces first public relations row.

text.p: A small group of protesters picketed the office of Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa on Monday, joining in on accusations of a possible conflict of interest within his handpicked team of advisers.

With just 99 days to go until Hong Kong is handed over to China, Tung faced his first real test of how to handle public opinion in the row over his decision last week to allocate "portfolios" to three members of his Executive Council.

Tung, anointed leader-in-waiting by a China-assembled panel in December, named property surveyer and real estate consultant Leung Chun-ying, one of 15 members of his Executive Council, as head of a committee to map out long-term housing strategy.
British governors picked their Executive Council members from all walks of life to tap a range of expertise, but did not hand out specific responsibilities.
Leung's appointment has angered many citizens who fear a conflict of interest and have vocally expressed their opposition, jamming radio talk shows and writing to newspapers.

Ten protesters spent their lunch hour on Monday making their anger known, shouting slogans including, "Oppose officials and businessmen collaborating" and, "We are opposed to real estate developers running Hong Kong".
They demanded Leung either resign from his own firm or stand down from the housing committee.
Hong Kong's democratic lobby voiced similar concerns.
"Mr Leung is a surveyor. It is explicit there is going to be a conflict of interest," Democratic Party legislator Lee Wing-tat said by telephone.
Housing is a sensitive issue in tiny but crowded Hong Kong, where housing costs are among the highest in the world.

The average wage for a clerical jobs is around HK$10,300 a month (US$1,300). A small flat in one of Hong Kong's massive new developments, typical for a first time buyer, costs around HK$3 million ($385,000).
The other two appointments -- to formulate policy on education and welfare -- have not drawn public anger.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than a century and a half, reverts to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.
